item.title: Conceptual Design of a 5 MV High-Voltage System for a Compact Orbitron Fusion Device
item.description: arXiv:2611.28658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The high-voltage system is a key part of the puzzle toward achieving net-positive fusion power in a compact Orbitron device. This paper presents a conceptual engineering design for a 5 MV, 20 mA, 100 kW HV system for a next-generation Orbitron, serving as an upper-bound design point for the HV system. The MC-TRANS++ 0-D code is used to set the load requirements: a 1 m long, 0.45 m first-wall-radius central cell, 2.5 T on-axis and 10 T mirror-throat fields, and a 5 MV radial potential drop sustaining supersonic rotation ($M = 4.8$). This delivers a triple product of $5.8 \times 10^{21}$ keV s /m3 and $Q_{sci}$ = 8.5. The HV power supply integrates an AC-DC converter, a SiC full-bridge inverter, a CLLC resonant network with an air-core step-up transformer, and feeds a 120-stage parallel-fed series-cascaded rectifier operating at 250 kHz. At full load, this architecture yields an end-to-end efficiency of 85%, much higher than the 60% typical of triode-driven MV-class power supplies. The 5 MV voltage is delivered to a radially nested 50-gap bushing system that interfaces pressurized insulating gas to high vacuum, using brazed alumina spacers with a corrugated profile. The design draws directly on the measured behavior of a previously demonstrated 300 kV prototype, from which six quantitative lessons are extracted and mapped onto the 5 MV design. Electrostatic simulations of the complete assembly at rated voltage show maximum surface fields of 30.3 MV/m on the corona rings, 7.7 MV/m at the cathode triple junction, and average vacuum-gap fields ranging from 5.5 to 40 MV/m. These field strengths remain below breakdown thresholds due to the implementation of triple-junction shielding, insulation corrugation, and axial magnetic insulation at 2.5-10 T. The conceptual system has a form factor of 2.7 meters in diameter and 6.5 meters in length, projected to deliver a net power output of 86-171 kWe.
item.dc:creator: Moein Borghei, Robin Langtry, Nicola Van Moon, Matthew Affolter, Erik McKee

item.title: Analysis of Geometric Eigenmode Splitting in Planar Microwave Resonators
item.description: arXiv:2611.29200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A traditional challenge in planar microwave resonator design is to find geometric mechanisms that can control individual resonant frequencies - or tune coupling between specific eigenmodes - without affecting other system parameters, such as the center frequency. Achieving this capability can be transformative for the design of microwave sensors, filters, antennas and resonant networks. Starting from first principles, we outline the development of an analytical method that guides practical design by suggesting specific perturbation shapes capable of achieving resonant mode-splitting while keeping the center frequency nearly stationary. This approach opens the door to novel designs that were previously difficult to discover or optimize. Independent numerical simulations and measurements of stripline resonators validate the effectiveness of this approach. The demonstrated tuning effect shows that the first-order estimate suggested by the theory persists in practice over a relatively wide splitting bandwidth (exceeding 54% of center frequency), increasing the utility of the proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Hagen Papenburg, Jason Corn, Romain Speciel, Adham Naji

item.title: Observation of collective flatbands in hybrid Mie-grating THz metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.28246v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a novel type of functional metasurfaces created by a hybridization of Mie resonators with high-index optical gratings. We demonstrate that such hybrid metasurfaces possess flatbands characterized by zero group velocity and strong energy localization. We experimentally observe the flatbands in free-standing terahertz (THz) metasurfaces, where dielectric interconnections between Mie resonators, forming the grating, mediate multipolar hybridization and provide a geometric control over collective resonances. Our THz near-field measurements with a dipole excitation uncover long-lived coherent oscillations associated with the quasi-flat magnetic-dipolar resonant modes, while a spatial mapping resolves the resonant electromagnetic response across the dielectric interconnections. We vary the grating width continuously to tune the hybrid magnetic-dipolar resonances and substantially enhance the quality factor (Q factor), while preserving the quasi-!atband dispersion. Complementary Bloch-resolved Purcell calculations reveal the substantial Purcell enhancement with increasing Q factor, followed by a trend towards saturation and highlighting the interplay between radiative confinement and local emitter-mode coupling. We believe our findings establish the engineering of dielectric interconnections in periodic lattices as a novel strategy for spectrally tuning high-Q flatbands in these metastructures, tailoring localized electromagnetic interactions in functional optical metasurfaces.
item.dc:creator: Jie Ji, Thanh Xuan Hoang, Ayan Nussupbekov, Siyan Zhou, Kehan Wang, Yuri Kivshar, Jaime G\'omez Rivas

item.title: Competing climates of the present-day Earth: from Snowball to Hothouse
item.description: arXiv:2611.28357v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Earth today has one climate, but it could have others. With the same continents, the same solar constant and the same pre-industrial CO2, our planet could settle into strikingly different ones. We explore this possibility with BIG-MITgcm, a model which couples atmosphere and ocean circulation with ice sheets and vegetation, and which can be integrated over many millennia. We find five different climates and describe them here. At one extreme is a Snowball, with ice from pole to pole. A Waterbelt also exists, in which sea ice reaches the tropics and only a thin equatorial ribbon of open ocean survives. There is a Cold world much like the Last Glacial Maximum, a Warm climate in which we live in today, and a Hot world in which the Atlantic overturning circulation has collapsed. Each state is held in place by its own balance of competing feedbacks. Ocean heat transport anchors each climate, holding the ice edge where that transport is weak. The familiar climate of the past 10 thousand years is perhaps just one of several possibilities. This has implications for glacial-interglacial transitions and the risk of crossing global tipping points in the future.
item.dc:creator: Laure Moinat, John Marshall, Maura Brunetti

item.title: Distinguishing photothermal and photoelectrokinetic contributions to flow in light-activated microchannel architectures
item.description: arXiv:2611.28481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Light-driven flows near Janus surfaces could power microfluidic devices without external hardware. These flows are often attributed to photoinduced electro- or diffusio-osmosis, but illumination also heats the surface, potentially driving natural convection. Here, we map flow and temperature around a UVA-illuminated TiO$_2$-Au Janus membrane using depth-resolved particle tracking and infrared thermometry. Recirculating rolls form on both sides, with no measurable net flow across the membrane. Their cubic, reversing velocity profile identifies horizontal (Hadley) convection, driven by a lateral temperature gradient as the gold film absorbs light. The measured profile agrees with wall-corrected Hadley theory using one fitted parameter. Adding 100 mM NaCl to suppress electrokinetic flows leaves the profile unchanged, indicating that convection dominates. Simulations show that convection falls below 1 $\mu$m/s in thin channels, where surface-driven osmotic flows could dominate. Thus, device geometry and surface chemistry determine which mechanism governs light-driven microfluidic flows.
item.dc:creator: Sudharshan Anandan, Yuhang Fang, Lily Farmer, Maria Irineu, Shanmukhi Sripada, Tyler Hughes, Jared Nathan, Sathish Rajendran, Steven Wereley, Amy Marconnet, Thomas Beechem, Jeffrey L. Moran, David M. Warsinger

item.title: Efficient phase-only wavefront shaping at 250 kHz for multimode fiber endomicroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2611.29015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wavefront shaping through multimode fibers (MMFs) enables diffraction-limited fluorescence imaging with hair-thin probes, at a speed and light budget bounded by the wavefront modulator. Existing modulators provide at most two of three key characteristics: high refresh rate, (high) modal dimensionality, and light efficiency. Here, we demonstrate wavefront control through an MMF using a tailored phase-only microelectromechanical modulator that combines all three, with 8,192 elements arranged in a 32 x 256 array, 7-bit phase control, and a 250 kHz full-frame refresh rate. Direct on-axis phase modulation delivers 70+/-5% of the incident light into the modulated field and eliminates both off-axis encoding optical losses and hologram computation. The generated foci at the distal end of the fiber remain isotropic with high fidelity. We use singular-value decomposition analysis of the measured transmission to identify the effective degrees of freedom of our system. By scanning the focus at multiple depths, we demonstrate volumetric fluorescence imaging. These results open a new operating regime for adaptive in vivo multimode-fiber endoscopy.
item.dc:creator: Pau Riera Rodr\'iguez, Antonio M. Caravaca-Aguirre, Omer Tzang, Alexander Payne, Stephen Hamann, Rafael Piestun

item.title: Uniguided and unicoupled resonances in an asymmetric acoustic metasurface
item.description: arXiv:2611.29078v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We theoretically study an acoustic metasurface that exhibits ultimate asymmetry in absorption under oblique incidence. This behavior arises from a counter-propagating pair of uniguided (UGR) and unicoupled (UCR) resonances. The UGR radiates to only one side, while the UCR radiates to both sides but can be excited from only one. In the lossless regime, the transmission phase winds by $2\pi$ across both UCR and UGR while the transmittance remains flat at any prescribed nonzero level. Thermoviscous losses introduce resonant intensity modulation and enable critical coupling, yielding perfect sound absorption exclusively for incidence through the channel that excites the UCR. Therefore, asymmetric metasurfaces with UCR and UGR offer a route to full phase control and perfect sound absorption.
item.dc:creator: Andrey S. Konchakov, Daniil S. Buzin, Dmitrii N. Maksimov, Mingzhao Song, Y. Li, Mikhail I. Petrov, Chao Peng, Andrey A. Bogdanov, Pavel S. Pankin

item.title: Polarization-independent self-hybridized strong coupling by Brillouin zone folding induced quasi-bound states in the continuum in bulk WS2 metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.29204v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-refractive-index dielectric metasurfaces supporting optical modes are ideal candidates for achieving strong coupling with transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) materials. However, optical illumination with a specific polarization is always required to estimate the maximal coupling strength in such coupled systems due to the polarization-dependent optical modes. Here, we propose a self-hybridized strong coupling between Brillouin zone folding induced quasi-bound states in the continuum (BZF-QBICs) mode and A excitons in the same bulk WS2 metasurface. By changing the thickness of the bulk WS2 metasurfaces, a typical anticrossing behavior with Rabi splitting of 165.9 meV is observed. Such Rabi splitting is unchanged when changing the polarization of the incident light from linearly to circularly polarizations, demonstrating the polarization-independent self-hybridized strong coupling. This work provides a novel method for realizing robust polarization-independent polaritons in bulk TMDCs metasurface and offers new insights for expanding the applications of polaritonic devices with arbitrary polarizations.
item.dc:creator: Xiongwei Guo, Fu Liu, Jinhai Si, Xun Hou, Kuidong Wang

item.title: A Theoretical Investigation of Magnetic Susceptibility Measurement of Diamagnetic Liquids Using a Michelson Interferometer
item.description: arXiv:2611.29671v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We examine the theoretical use of a Michelson interferometer to infer the magnetic susceptibility of a diamagnetic liquid from a magnetically induced surface deformation. A ring magnet changes the liquid thickness along the sample beam, producing a signed phase shift relative to a fixed optical reference. For a double traversal of the sample, the fringe displacement is $m = 2(n_{\ell} - n_a)\Delta z/\lambda$. We derive the susceptibility inversion both in a local gravity approximation and with surface tension included through the linearized Young-Laplace equation. The treatment distinguishes a finite reference field from a zero-field reference, specifies the displacement sign and susceptibility contrast, and identifies calibration and uncertainty requirements. Reproducible illustrative calculations use a uniformly magnetized annulus. The results establish a theoretical measurement relation and its assumptions; they do not constitute an experimental demonstration or a verified accuracy claim.
item.dc:creator: David Shulman

item.title: Pyroelectric Harvesting from Steady Heat Sources via Active Piezoelectric Thermal Switching
item.description: arXiv:2611.29928v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study demonstrates pyroelectric energy harvesting from a steady heat source using active piezoelectric thermal switching in a PZT/Si bimorph cantilever. The same PZT layer serves as both the mechanical actuator and the pyroelectric energy-conversion element. Dual output electrodes enable separation of the pyroelectric and piezoelectric signals. Pyroelectric energy harvesting is experimentally demonstrated at frequencies up to 110 Hz and temperature differences as small as 5 K. Comparison with the response predicted from the independently measured pyroelectric coefficient, together with transient thermal simulations, identifies dynamic interfacial heat transfer as a key limitation to high-frequency operation. This work demonstrates a compact MEMS approach for higher-frequency pyroelectric energy harvesting from low-grade steady heat sources.
item.dc:creator: Jun Usami, Yuki Okamoto, Shimpei Saito, Saeko Tachikawa, Soumei Baba, Takeshi Fujii, Sucheta Gorwadkar, Natsumi Makimoto, Takeshi Kobayashi

item.title: Designing Incoherent Multispectral Diffractive Optical Networks for Satellite Image Classification
item.description: arXiv:2611.30079v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optical neural networks and diffractive optical computing provide a promising route for performing task-specific inference with high parallelism and lightweight electronic post-processing. These advantages are especially attractive for multispectral satellite imaging, where conventional workflows rely on transmitting high-dimensional image cubes to the ground for downstream electronic analysis. Here, we introduce a computationally efficient surrogate model-guided framework for designing incoherent multispectral diffractive optical networks that directly output class probabilities onboard, eliminating the need to capture and transfer the full multispectral data cube for ground-side inference. We first train a physically compatible surrogate model, represented by a non-negative fully connected model that accommodates a generalized detector readout, yielding a task-specific non-negative multispectral intensity transformation that can be transferred to an optical processor. We then synthesize its diffractive counterpart through data-free point-spread-function-based optimization under spatially incoherent illumination. Using this approach, we numerically demonstrate a six-spectral-channel diffractive classifier for tri-class satellite-scene recognition, achieving a blind-testing accuracy of 79.8% for artificial surface, water body, and vegetated land images, closely approaching the 81.8% accuracy of its surrogate. We further demonstrate a more compact three-spectral-channel design that numerically achieves 72.7% blind-testing accuracy, compared with 75.1% for its corresponding surrogate model. This surrogate model-guided strategy provides a practical pathway for designing compact, task-specific incoherent multispectral optical processors for resource-constrained remote-sensing inference.
item.dc:creator: Xilin Yang, Md Sadman Sakib Rahman, Ryan Lee, Aydogan Ozcan

item.title: Apparent thermal conductivity governed by interface-injected phonon spectra
item.description: arXiv:2611.30276v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Thermoreflectance techniques such as time- and frequency-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR and FDTR) are widely used to measure the thermal conductivity of bulk materials, thin films, and interfaces. When phonon mean free paths $\Lambda_\omega$ become comparable to the thermal penetration depth, a Fourier analysis yields an apparent thermal conductivity $\kappa_{\rm app}$ that deviates from the bulk value $\kappa_{\rm bulk}$. Recent studies have highlighted the role of the phonon spectrum injected through the transducer interface, which is generally out of equilibrium owing to frequency-dependent transmission, and have shown that accounting for this nonequilibrium distribution can yield $\kappa_{\rm app}>\kappa_{\rm bulk}$, unlike conventional suppression-function analyses that predict only $\kappa_{\rm app}\leq\kappa_{\rm bulk}$. However, the spectral characteristics governing whether $\kappa_{\rm app}$ is enhanced or reduced remain unclear. Here, we resolve the surface-temperature response of semi-infinite Si mode by mode and show that short-$\Lambda_\omega$-weighted injection raises the surface temperature, whereas long-$\Lambda_\omega$-weighted injection lowers it. This behavior is governed by how deep the injected phonons travel before thermalizing with the lattice, which is set by their mean free paths, and by how effectively the substrate conducts the injected energy away, which is limited by its long-mean-free-path phonons. For an Al (70 nm)/Si structure, Fourier fits of synthetic TDTR phase signals give $\kappa_{\rm app}$ of Si from about 93 to 360 W/(m K) for different interfacial transmission spectra, and $\kappa_{\rm app}$ correlates with the heat-flux-weighted $\Lambda_\omega$ of the transmitted phonons. Thus, $\kappa_{\rm app}$ from thermoreflectance reflects not only the substrate thermal properties but also the phonon spectrum injected across the transducer interface.
item.dc:creator: D. G. Jeong, Terumasa Tadano, J. S. Lee

item.title: A Highly Tunable (Ti,Zr)N$_x$-Based MIM Plasmonic Sensor for Multidomain Biological, Chemical, and Physical Sensing
item.description: arXiv:2611.30614v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Metal-Insulator-Metal (MIM) plasmonic refractive index (RI) sensors have attracted considerable attention for label-free, real-time analyte detection; however, their reliance on noble metals such as gold and silver imposes fundamental constraints on tunability, thermal stability, and CMOS process compatibility. In this work, we propose a novel MIM plasmonic RI sensor based on a square ring resonator with embedded circular nanorods, employing the ternary nitride (Ti,Zr)N$_x$ as the plasmonic material, marking its first application in a MIM sensing platform. Compared to binary nitrides and other alternative plasmonic materials reported in the literature, (Ti,Zr)N$_x$ offers broader compositional tunability and greater flexibility in tailoring the optical response while remaining fully CMOS-compatible. The sensor is validated across a comprehensive range of biosensing and physicochemical analyte scenarios, including glucose monitoring for diabetes assessment, hemoglobin-based anemia classification across four severity levels, simultaneous discrimination of five major blood constituents, and cancer cell identification across six tissue types. For physical and chemical sensing, the structure achieves an air pressure sensitivity of 6.158 nm/MPa with negligible thermal cross-sensitivity, and a CO$_2$ detection sensitivity of 330.12 pm/ppm via polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) functionalization, which is the highest reported among comparable structures in the literature. The proposed sensor achieves a maximum RI sensitivity of 2146.496 nm/RIU with a detection limit of $4.669 \times 10^{-7}$ RIU, outperforming previously reported CMOS-compatible plasmonic RI sensors.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Abrar Kabir, Aosaf Jarif Siddiquee, Abdullah Taharat, A. K. M. Rakib, Rakibul Hasan Sagor

item.title: Solute-Aware Stochastic Korhonen Model of Electromigration in Wide vs Near-Bamboo Al-Cu Lines
item.description: arXiv:2611.31206v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We couple an evolving Cu field to the one-dimensional Korhonen stress equation on random grain maps for wide (10 $\mu$m), narrow (3 $\mu$m) and near-bamboo Al-Cu lines. Earlier random-microstructure simulations fixed the Cu effect, and most continuum solute models used prescribed structures with all Cu mobile; we join the two and let only dissolved Cu move, the excess staying as immobile precipitate. With $10^3$ maps per condition at 200 $^\circ$C, we report nucleation times and sites, immortal fractions and Black's-law parameters. In cathode-limited lines Cu depletion shortens the median nucleation time 1.15- to 1.20-fold relative to immobile Cu for the cited Cu diffusivity; treating all Cu as mobile overstates this a further 2.24- to 2.36-fold at 2 wt%; the exponent stays near 2. In wide lines with reservoir ends, Cu steps left by the immobile precipitate become the failure sites, removing their Cu-free immortality if a quarter or more of the precipitate blocks Al diffusion. With Cu above the solvus the lifetime is not Arrhenius, as the dissolved fraction rises with temperature: a Black's-law fit at 250 to 300 $^\circ$C overestimates the median nucleation time at 150 $^\circ$C up to 2.33-fold at 2 wt% Cu with an exponent near 2. At the test durations the model qualitatively matches the cathode-side damage in narrow lines and the Cu build-up and mid-line peaks in wide lines but not the cathode-side Cu peaks or longer lives of narrow lines.
item.dc:creator: Narahara Chari Dingari, David R. Heskett

item.title: Physics-Based Learning of the Wave Speed Landscape in Complex Media
item.description: arXiv:2602.03281v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The propagation of waves through complex, inhomogeneous media is a fundamental challenge across scales, from optics to geophysics. In such environments, the waves reflected by the medium are typically dominated by a random speckle pattern, a complex interference resulting from multiple scattering by fine-scale heterogeneities. While this speckle is traditionally viewed as a source of noise that blurs the medium's structure, it contains rich information about the underlying wave speed landscape. Here, we introduce a physics-based learning framework that reconstructs the velocity distribution from the reflection matrix of the medium. We show how the speckle wave-field can be exploited to probe the focusing quality, serving as an intrinsic guide star to evaluate the local consistency of the velocity model. By representing wave propagation as a differentiable multi-layer network, we leverage optimization tools to solve the inverse problem and infer the wave speed map. We validate this approach through ultrasound experiments in highly scattering tissue-mimicking phantoms and human breast tissues, demonstrating its potential for tumor detection and characterization where standard methods fail. This synergy between wave physics and gradient-based optimization provides a general paradigm for non-invasive tomography in any complex environment where reflection data is available.
item.dc:creator: Baptiste H\'eriard-Dubreuil, Emma Brenner, Benjamin Rio, William Lambert, Foucauld Chamming's, Mathias Fink, Alexandre Aubry

item.title: Lithium Niobate Surface-Acoustic-Wave Resonator for Very-High-Frequency Isolated Power Conversion
item.description: arXiv:2610.02742v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Piezoelectric devices offer a promising magnetic-free alternative for high-frequency power conversion. Here, we demonstrate a lithium niobate surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonator that is optimized for isolated power transfer and show advantages in operating frequency, power density, power handling, and electrical isolation. Our application-optimized 40-MHz SAW resonator, with two electrically isolated interdigital transducers (IDTs) and acoustic Bragg mirrors, achieves a 25.7 W output power at a temperature rise of about 15 {\deg}C with only passive cooling through the back mounting side. With a chip size of 0.095 cm$^3$ and an acoustic mode volume of 0.00255 cm$^3$, our device features a peak chip power density of 270.5 W/cm$^3$ and a mode-volume power density of 10,078 W/cm$^3$. Our device shows an isolation voltage of 2.17 kV. Driven by a GaN full-bridge inverter, our device can drive different load resistors with a calculated peak power transfer efficiency of 87.5%. Our results show the potential of SAW devices as a core component for next-generation power systems.
item.dc:creator: Liyang Jin, Zhiyang Cao, Zichen Xi, Jun Ji, Yizheng Zhu, Liyan Zhu, Linbo Shao

item.title: An Innovative Photon-Driven Subcritical Reactor Concept Powered by Synchrotron Radiation Source
item.description: arXiv:2509.01249v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most reactors are fuelled with enriched uranium, whose production is proliferation-sensitive and concentrated in a few suppliers, and discharge fuel that still contains fissile material and accumulates in storage. Accelerator-driven subcritical reactors relax the requirements on the fuel, but proton beams must travel in vacuum to a spallation target inside the core. Here we show that synchrotron radiation can drive a subcritical heavy-water reactor fuelled with natural uranium or with spent fuel loaded without reprocessing. A photon beam with a critical energy of 10 MeV, from a proposed 32 GeV electron storage ring, releases neutrons in a uranium converter at the centre of the core. Coupled photon-neutron Monte Carlo simulations show that the two cores, loading different fuels but being at a multiplication factor close to 0.985, reach the same gain: one 400 kW beamline drives each of them close to 4.4 MW of fission power, about 11 times the beam power. A storage ring with 50 beamlines could drive one core from each beamline, every core controlled through its own photon beam. These results make synchrotron radiation a candidate driver for thermal subcritical reactors that need neither enrichment nor reprocessing, complementary to proton-driven fast systems for transmutation.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Cammi, Lorenzo Loi, Andrea Missaglia, David Alesini, Hans-Heinrich Braun

item.title: Thin-Film AlN Microbolometer for Very-Long-Wave Infrared Detection
item.description: arXiv:2604.22301v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We demonstrate a suspended thin-film aluminum nitride (AlN) microbolometer for narrowband very-long-wave infrared detection. The device uses a 100 nm-thick AlN membrane suspended above a Pt back reflector by a 1 $\mu$m air gap. Resonant absorption near 15.4 $\mu$m is set by the AlN transverse optical phonon and is strengthened by suspension above the reflector. A periodic perforation pattern reduces membrane thermal mass, facilitates release, and tunes the effective optical thickness without requiring a thinner deposited film. Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) reflection measurements on the released bolometer show approximately 95% peak cavity absorptance near 15.4 $\mu$m with a 0.772 $\mu$m FWHM. DC resistance measurements under tunable infrared illumination verify bolometric operation, with a peak normalized resistive responsivity of 252 ppm/mW at 15.48 $\mu$m. This platform can enable compact wavelength-selective thermal detectors for multispectral imaging, on-chip infrared spectroscopy, and chemical sensing.
item.dc:creator: Vivek Tallavajhula, Zarko Sakotic, Ian Anderson, Yinan Wang, Daniel Wasserman, Ruochen Lu

item.title: High-Power Laser Drives Motion in Ultra-thin Photonic Crystal Lightsails
item.description: arXiv:2606.20149v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Laser-driven lightsails require reflectors that are ultralight, highly reflective and robust under intense illumination. These demands point to the thinnest reflectors that dielectric optics allows, photonic crystals, in which a perforated membrane thinner than the wavelength of light acts as a mirror. Such mirrors reflect by confining light inside the membrane, but this confinement also amplifies absorption, making ultralow-loss, tension-bearing materials essential. Stoichiometric high-stress silicon nitride uniquely meets both requirements, yet its ~1 GPa stress makes large, compliant structures difficult to release intact, and such sails have never been pushed by high-power lasers. Here we demonstrate millimeter-wide, 200-nm-thick photonic-crystal trampolines in this material, with 99% design reflectivity at 1070 nm and a static stiffness of 0.53 N/m. Radiation pressure displaces them by more than a micrometer within 50 microseconds. In air, they withstand several times the irradiance found at the Sun's surface, delivered as a coherent beam. Light reshapes the sail more than it pushes it, since modest temperature differences buckle the membrane and collapse its stiffness, so thermal deformation outpaces radiation pressure within milliseconds. The interaction and compliance that make lightsails movable also let light deform them. These results establish a testbed for high-power nanophotonics, directed-energy systems and light-driven propulsion.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Norder, Ata Ke\c{s}kekler, Richard A. Norte

item.title: Impact of Channel Dynamics on Higher-order Interactions of Oscillators
item.description: arXiv:2607.07662v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modeling higher-order interactions (HOIs) in nonlinear networks with static topologies is often physically restrictive. We demonstrate that standard 3-body Kuramoto couplings are mathematically equivalent to pairwise connections modulated by latent variables of transmission channels. While standard HOI topologies emerge in the adiabatic limit of these variables, relaxing this constraint reveals that latent channel timescales dictate collective macroscopic states. Specifically, transmission inertia drives bistability for symmetric interaction tensors and anti-phase cluster synchronization for antisymmetric ones. Furthermore, dynamically induced clustering in global topologies emerges as a finite-size effect of the dynamics of the local channels. Ultimately, we show that relying exclusively on static topologies restricts interaction modeling. Integrating latent variables captures the transient inertia and fundamental asymmetry of physical networks, bridging the analytical utility of higher-order functions with the reality of the underlying transmission medium.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Marghoti, Isabela A. Martins, Giovana S. Spezzatto, Emanuel B. S. A. Cambraia, Sergio R. Lopes, Thiago L. Prado

item.title: Microscopically informed constitutive framework for stress overshoot, yielding, and strain hardening in amorphous materials
item.description: arXiv:2607.13734v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a microscopic constitutive theory for the nonlinear deformation of metallic and polymer glasses based on nonaffine elasticity coupled to irreversible many-body relaxation. The theory predicts the full stress--strain response, from linear elasticity through stress overshoot and yielding to steady plastic flow. We show that stress overshoot originates from the competition between a nonaffine elastic instability induced by strain-driven loss of mechanical connectivity at the atomic/molecular level, and viscous dissipation associated with structural relaxation. For polymer glasses, finite chain extensibility naturally accounts for strain hardening at large deformation. The stretched-exponential relaxation exponent is obtained independently from stress or modulus relaxation measurements and provides the primary dynamical input to the theory. Using a small set of physically meaningful parameters, the model quantitatively reproduces experimental stress--strain curves for metallic glasses, polycarbonate, PMMA, and epoxy resins over a broad range of strain rates. These results establish a unified microscopic framework linking relaxation dynamics, yielding, plastic flow, and strain hardening in amorphous solids.
item.dc:creator: Ankit Singh, Valeriy V. Ginzburg, Alessio Zaccone

item.title: Evaluating LLM-based AI agents integrated with materials synthesis tools: the case of atomic layer deposition
item.description: arXiv:2608.29309v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work provides an overview of the different strategies that can be used to evaluate the performance of AI models and agents based on large language models (LLMs) for materials synthesis. After providing a brief overview of the key technologies behind the current generation of AI agents based on LLMs, we summarize the different approaches to evaluating these models in the context of materials science and in particular on materials synthesis, with a specific emphasis on scenarios in which the models are directly integrated with experimental tools. We discuss evaluation strategies spanning knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, tool-use benchmarks, and closed loop benchmarks involving the interaction with experimental systems or realistic virtual tools. We use atomic layer deposition (ALD) as a case study, emphasizing how existing approaches in the literature both build from general approaches used beyond materials science and can be generalized to other materials synthesis techniques. Finally, we provide a practical evaluation framework to evaluate LLMs in the context of materials synthesis
item.dc:creator: Angel Yanguas-Gil

item.title: Heteroepitaxial Growth of PbSe on InP via III-V Buffer Layers
item.description: arXiv:2609.09605v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Detector cost remains a barrier to the widespread adoption of mid-wave infrared (3-5 micron) technology. PbSe, an inexpensive narrow band gap IV-VI semiconductor that has been used since the early 1940s, delivers high performance for infrared detection despite the abundance of grain boundaries in polycrystalline films. Epitaxial growth, however, could provide superior crystalline quality and interfaces, but suitable substrates remain limited for PbSe. Recent PbSe heteroepitaxy has focused primarily on III-V, II-VI and group-IV substrates that each offer a comparatively narrow range of lattice-matched alloys for heterostructure engineering. Here we show that InP-based heteroepitaxy provides access to a broader materials platform while limiting the lattice mismatch with PbSe to approximately 4%. We grow 151-nm thick PbSe films by molecular beam epitaxy on 200-nm thick In0.53Ga0.47As and In0.52Al0.48As buffers on (001) InP substrates. Reflection high-energy electron diffraction and X-ray diffraction show (001)-oriented rock-salt PbSe with an out-of-plane lattice constant of 6.12 Angstrom on both buffers. Photoluminescence (PL) is observed from room-temperature down to 12 K and the peak wavelength red-shifts from 3.7 to 5.0 microns. Under identical measurement conditions, the room-temperature peak PL intensities from films on In0.53Ga0.47As and In0.52Al0.48As are approximately 1.9x and 1.3x that of a PbSe on GaAs substrate reference, respectively. These results establish an InP-compatible platform for integrating narrow band-gap PbSe with a broad range of ternary and quaternary III-V alloys, including, for example, structures in which In0.53Ga0.47As serves as both a short-wave infrared absorber and a template for PbSe growth.

item.title: Goal-Oriented Wave Computing for Direction-of-Arrival Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2610.06839v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Programmable metasurfaces are arrays of elements whose electromagnetic response can be tuned electronically. They can process signals as a wave propagates through or reflects off them, an approach known as wave-domain analog computing, or wave computing. The design strategy is typically indirect: the surface is fitted to a prescribed linear operator, such as a discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and the result is read from output power measurements. Using direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation as a canonical benchmark, we study what this indirection costs across three analog computing topologies: reflective reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS), beyond-diagonal RIS (BD-RIS), and stacked intelligent metasurfaces (SIM). We first derive Cram\'er-Rao bounds for the complete physical estimation chain, including one that accounts for output detectors measuring only intensity. We then formulate a goal-oriented alternative where the surfaces are trained directly through the deployed readout, with no operator target. We observe that goal-oriented training lets sparsely connected or shallower surfaces reach the task performance of their more complex operator-fitted counterparts, despite nearly identical Fisher information. For fully connected BD-RIS and six-layer SIM, the advantage persists under one- and two-bit control. From 16 to 64 elements, the connectivity a beyond-diagonal RIS needs grows with the aperture, and the depth saving of a stacked intelligent metasurface shrinks. Under tuner and per-layer loss, the goal-oriented designs mostly keep their advantage over DFT fits of the same hardware.
